query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of interstitial elements (such as oxygen or nitrogen) into the HEA composition creates ordered interstitial complexes that simultaneously increase solid‐solution/precipitation strengthening and enhance strain hardening, leading to concurrent improvement in both strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A base high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) without significant interstitial doping exhibiting moderate yield strength (~810 MPa) and limited ductility (~10% elongation).
generation.intervention: Interstitial doping by adding a controlled quantity of oxygen or nitrogen during alloy processing, which promotes the formation of ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs).
generation.conditions: Standard casting and remelting procedures (e.g., arc-melting, drop casting) under high-purity argon with repeated melting for homogenization; subsequent processing and heat treatment that permit the interstitial atoms to order within the distorted BCC matrix.
generation.structural_mediator: Ordered interstitial complexes dispersed within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The interstitial atoms preferentially form ordered complexes that act as nano-scale obstacles to dislocation motion (enhancing yield strength via precipitation/solid–solution strengthening) while also avoiding the formation of a continuous brittle ordered phase, thus preserving or even enhancing ductility by supporting effective strain hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the un-doped base alloy, the interstitial-doped alloy is expected to show a significant increase in yield strength (by several hundred MPa) along with improved ductility (increased percent elongation), resulting in a more balanced strength–ductility performance.
generation.baseline: The base alloy processed without interstitial doping, which exhibits lower yield strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on achieving an optimal interstitial content and ordered complex fraction; excessive interstitial addition may lead to excessive contamination or formation of brittle phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact fraction of ordered complexes required for the best strength–ductility balance is sensitive to processing conditions and alloy composition. Quantitative improvements (e.g., exact MPa or % elongation gains) remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the same base HEA: one without interstitial doping and one with a controlled addition of oxygen/nitrogen. Process both batches under identical conditions (arc-melting with repeated remelting, drop cast into identical molds) and subject them to the same heat treatments. Measure and compare mechanical properties (yield strength and elongation) of both groups.
measurements: Tensile tests to obtain yield strength and total elongation
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, APT) to confirm the presence and distribution of ordered interstitial complexes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interstitial-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in both yield strength and ductility compared to the base alloy, or if microstructural analysis shows no formation of ordered interstitial complexes, then the hypothesis that interstitial doping concurrently improves both strength and ductility is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
